params.title: Recurring methane, south Caspian site near Krasnovodsk
params.place: Arid desert terrain near Krasnovodsk, Turkmenistan, with a small settlement and linear infrastructure features visible on the ground.
observations: EMIT looked at this site 24 times from 2022-08-15 to 2025-08-20.
NASA outlined methane plumes here on 4 dates (2023-06-20, 2023-10-09, 2024-08-12, 2024-10-05), with a peak of 4,096 ppm·m and a rate of 2,567.3 kg/h on 2024-10-05.
EMIT's own passes since 2025-01-01 show 4 candidates on 4 separate dates, with peaks of 1,916.0, 4,325.9, 9,144.0, and 4,353.6 ppm·m.
The strongest candidate on 2025-08-01 had 1,346 pixels at or above 1,000 ppm·m and 1,162 pixels above 3x uncertainty.
TROPOMI recorded a 122.9 ppb anomaly over this site in the 14 days to 2026-09-23, the highest of all watch areas scanned.

explanations.next_check: Repeated enhancement on multiple dates without gaps would support this; ground inspection or aircraft survey could confirm or rule it out.
A sudden increase in peak ppm·m relative to prior passes, or a change in plume location, would indicate this.
Thermal infrared imagery or night-time VIIRS data showing no persistent heat source would help rule this out.
Enhancement on 4 separate dates spanning months makes a single blowdown less consistent; repeat aircraft passes would clarify.
Sentinel-2 shows arid terrain with no wetlands or agriculture; a ground survey would confirm the absence of biogenic sources.

gaps: NASA's plume product is nearly empty after 2024, so passes since late 2024 have not been independently outlined.
EMIT only observes on its orbital passes and cannot provide continuous monitoring.
No wind-based flux estimates are available for the 2025 candidate passes.
Sentinel-2 imagery shows structures but cannot identify the specific source of methane enhancement.
params.next_collection: A dedicated EMIT overpass or airborne survey over the Krasnovodsk site would confirm recurrence and provide a flux estimate.
